nielsen: Read heuristics 1–3, 5–7 and 9. Supports familiar terminology, visible state, prevention, recovery and expert shortcuts. These are broad heuristics, not proof of a particular layout.
vv: Jeff Stewart · Build Great Tools, GDC 2018

Read PDF pp.25–26, 33–36 and 40–46: grouping and adjacent workflow, content models, undo, preview and recovery. Stewart explicitly cites Nielsen on p.33: this is a production application of that principle, not an independent experiment.
mk: Read PDF pp.45–49. QA feedback led to both-player controls and frame stepping in the tool. The case documents an iteration, not a controlled comparison or a Python implementation.
testing: Read Elements of Usability Testing, Tasks and Participants. Supports realistic tasks and observing behavior while avoiding coaching. Pair with the production case and local peer-test observations.
proximity: Aurora Harley · Proximity Principle in Visual Design, NN/G
Read Close Proximity Indicates Relatedness and the grouped-form illustration. Supports using spacing to communicate relationships. It does not supply a measured gain for our Unreal interface.
layout: Read Grouping, Alignment and sizing/resizing guidance. Use relationships and hierarchy; do not import legacy Windows styling, numeric spacing rules or group-count limits into Qt/Slate as universal requirements. The page identifies its Windows 7 origin.
keys: Read When to use keyboard accelerators, Scoped accelerators and menu-label examples. Supports discoverable shortcuts for frequent actions and explicit focus scope. The API examples are Windows APIs, not PySide or Unreal code.
errors: Read Characteristics of good error messages. Supports specific, actionable explanations. Use the message structure, not its dated visual styling; retain diagnostic detail separately when needed.

priorities: Highest priority: direct artist-tool example plus general guidance. Natoli 01–05 reinforces the framing.
State the intended outcome and use terms the artist can act on. Do not expose each internal function as a separate user decision.
Highest priority: directly relevant to tools that modify assets. Multiple guidance sources plus production practice.
Show affected objects, explain whether anything changed, and provide a recovery route that the tool actually supports.
Highest priority: method guidance plus a documented game-development iteration from a separate organization.
Give a realistic task, observe a difficulty, make a targeted revision and retest. Do not substitute preference votes for task evidence.
Strong visual addition: NN/G and Microsoft agree on grouping; Stewart discusses it in a content-tool context.
Use spacing and alignment to distinguish target, proposed change and action. Test the arrangement with the actual task.
Strong desktop addition: supports both learning and repeated work; directly counters a phone-only interpretation.
Keep a visible route to commands while providing discoverable shortcuts for frequent actions. Check focus and scope.

visuals.use: Place the full menu screenshot on the left; on the right ask students to identify the visible command and its shortcut. Do not present these keys as implemented in the course tool.
